days.title: Sex Chromosomes & Sex Determination
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Describe sex chromosomes.
  • Explain sex determination in humans.
  • Differentiate autosomes from sex chromosomes.
  • Identify disorders of sex chromosome number.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Autosomes — the 22 pairs of non-sex chromosomes.
  • Sex chromosomes — X and Y chromosomes.
  • XX — female; XY — male.
  • SRY gene — on Y chromosome; triggers male development.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Human Chromosomes

  • Total: 46 chromosomes (23 pairs)
  • 22 pairs = autosomes
  • 1 pair = sex chromosomes (XX or XY)

B. Sex Determination

The father determines the sex of the child — he can pass an X or a Y.

FatherMotherOffspring
XXXX (female)
YXXY (male)

C. Sex Chromosome Disorders

ConditionGenotype
Turner syndromeXO
Klinefelter syndromeXXY
Triple X syndromeXXX

💬 Let's Discuss

Humans have 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs. Twenty-two pairs are autosomes, which carry genes for most traits and look the same in males and females. The 23rd pair are the sex chromosomes: females are usually XX and males XY. The X is large and carries over 800 genes, many unrelated to sex (for blood clotting, color vision, muscle proteins). The Y is small and carries few genes, but one is crucial: the SRY gene (sex-determining region Y), which switches on development of testes. Without a working SRY, an embryo develops along the female pathway.

Who decides the baby's sex? Every egg carries an X. Sperm carry either an X or a Y, in about equal numbers. An X-bearing sperm gives an XX daughter; a Y-bearing sperm gives an XY son. So the father's sperm determines the sex, and each pregnancy has about a 50% chance of each — a Punnett square of XX × XY shows exactly this.

Errors in meiosis (nondisjunction) can change the number of sex chromosomes. Turner syndrome (45,X or XO): a female with one X; short height, underdeveloped ovaries, usually infertile. Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY): a male with an extra X; tall, small testes, reduced fertility. Triple X (47,XXX) females are often unaffected. These show that the Y (with SRY) decides maleness, not the number of X chromosomes.

Other species use other systems: in birds, females are ZW and males ZZ; in many turtles and crocodiles, the incubation temperature of the egg determines sex.

Common mistake: blaming the mother for having only daughters. Biologically, the sperm determines the baby's sex.

Turner syndrome is a female with a single X (45,X).
Klinefelter syndrome is a male with an extra X (47,XXY).

days.title: X-Linked Inheritance Patterns
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Explain X-linked inheritance.
  • Describe why males are more often affected.
  • Predict offspring from X-linked crosses.
  • Identify X-linked disorders.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • X-linked gene — gene carried on the X chromosome.
  • Hemizygous — males have only one X, so one allele determines the trait.
  • Carrier — a female with one recessive allele who doesn't show the trait.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Why Males Are Affected More

Males have only one X chromosome. If that X carries a recessive allele, the male will show the trait. Females must inherit two recessive alleles to be affected.

B. Examples of X-Linked Recessive Disorders

  • Hemophilia A
  • Red-green color blindness
  • Duchenne muscular dystrophy

C. Cross Example

Carrier mother (XᶜX) × normal father (XY):

  • Daughters: 50% carriers, 50% normal
  • Sons: 50% affected, 50% normal

💬 Let's Discuss

Genes located on the X chromosome are called X-linked. Because males and females carry different numbers of X chromosomes, X-linked traits are inherited in a special pattern.

A female (XX) has two copies of each X-linked gene. If she has one recessive allele, the normal allele on her other X usually covers for it, so she is an unaffected carrier. A male (XY) has only one X — he is hemizygous for X-linked genes, because the Y has no matching copy. Whatever allele is on his X shows up. That is why X-linked recessive disorders are much more common in males: one recessive allele is enough.

Write alleles as superscripts on X. For red–green color blindness: Xᴮ = normal, Xᵇ = color-blind. Carrier mother × normal father (XᴮXᵇ × XᴮY): daughters are 50% XᴮXᴮ and 50% carriers (none affected); sons are 50% normal and 50% affected. A son always gets his X from his mother and his Y from his father, so fathers never pass X-linked traits to sons, but they pass their X to every daughter. If the mother is affected (XᵇXᵇ), all sons are affected.

Examples: hemophilia A (blood fails to clot; it spread among European royal families from Queen Victoria, a carrier), red–green color blindness (about 8% of males), Duchenne muscular dystrophy, and G6PD deficiency, which is common in the Philippines and is screened through newborn screening.

Common mistake: thinking affected sons inherit the trait from their fathers. In X-linked inheritance, an affected son received the allele from his mother.

days.title: Y-Linked Traits & Sex-Linked Disorders
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Describe Y-linked traits.
  • Explain inheritance patterns of Y-linked traits.
  • Distinguish sex-linked from sex-influenced traits.
  • Identify common sex-linked disorders.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Y-linked — genes on the Y chromosome.
  • Holandric — passed from father to all sons.
  • Sex-influenced — trait expressed differently in males and females.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Y-Linked Traits

  • Only males have a Y chromosome
  • Traits passed father → all sons
  • Examples: hairy ears, some fertility genes

B. Sex-Influenced Traits

  • Autosomal genes, but expression differs by sex
  • Example: pattern baldness (more common in males)

C. Sex-Linked Disorders (Summary)

DisorderType
Hemophilia AX-linked recessive
Color blindnessX-linked recessive
Duchenne muscular dystrophyX-linked recessive
Hairy earsY-linked
Pattern baldnessSex-influenced

💬 Let's Discuss

Not every trait that differs between the sexes is X-linked. There are three other patterns to distinguish.

Y-linked (holandric) traits are controlled by genes on the Y chromosome. Since only males have a Y, these traits appear only in males and pass from a father to all of his sons — never to daughters. The Y has few genes, so true Y-linked traits are rare; examples include the SRY gene and some genes for sperm production (so certain types of male infertility are Y-linked). Hairy ears (hypertrichosis of the ear) is often taught as a Y-linked example, though its inheritance is still debated.

Sex-influenced traits are controlled by autosomal genes, but the same genotype is expressed differently in males and females because of hormones. Male-pattern baldness is the classic example: the baldness allele acts as dominant in males (one copy is enough, with testosterone present) but as recessive in females (two copies are needed). Women can inherit and pass on the allele.

Sex-limited traits are autosomal traits shown by only one sex because of anatomy or hormones — for example, milk production in female cattle or beard growth in men. Both sexes carry the genes.

To identify the pattern in a family: Father → all sons, never daughters? Think Y-linked. Carrier mothers → about half of sons affected, fathers never → sons? Think X-linked recessive. Both sexes carry it but one sex shows it more? Think sex-influenced.

Common mistake: calling baldness Y-linked because it is common in men. Baldness genes are on autosomes (and an X-linked gene also contributes); hormones explain the difference.

pairs.why: Y-linked genes are found on the Y chromosome.
Holandric traits pass from father to all of his sons.
Sex-influenced traits are autosomal but expressed differently in each sex.
Pattern baldness acts dominant in males and recessive in females.
Hairy ears is the classic textbook example of a Y-linked trait.
Hemophilia is carried on the X, not the Y.

days.title: Recombination & Gene Linkage
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Define genetic recombination.
  • Explain crossing over and its role.
  • Define gene linkage and map units.
  • Interpret recombination frequencies.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Recombination — new combinations of alleles from crossing over.
  • Linked genes — genes close together on the same chromosome.
  • Map unit (centimorgan) — 1% recombination frequency.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Recombination

During Prophase I of meiosis, homologous chromosomes exchange segments (crossing over). This creates new allele combinations.

B. Linked Genes

  • Genes on the same chromosome tend to be inherited together
  • The closer they are, the less likely they'll be separated by crossing over

C. Recombination Frequency

  • RF = (number of recombinants) / (total offspring) × 100%
  • 1% RF = 1 map unit (centimorgan)
  • Used to build genetic maps

💬 Let's Discuss

Mendel's law of independent assortment works perfectly for genes on different chromosomes. But each chromosome carries hundreds or thousands of genes. Genes that lie close together on the same chromosome are linked — they tend to be inherited together, like passengers in the same jeepney.

Linkage is not complete, because of crossing over in prophase I of meiosis. Homologous chromosomes swap segments, producing chromosomes with new combinations of alleles. Offspring with these new combinations are called recombinants; those with the parents' original combinations are parentals.

Thomas Hunt Morgan's student Alfred Sturtevant realized that the farther apart two genes are, the more likely a crossover will fall between them. So the recombination frequency (RF) can be used to measure distance:

RF = (number of recombinant offspring ÷ total offspring) × 100

One percent recombination equals 1 map unit, also called 1 centimorgan (cM). If 10 of 100 offspring are recombinant, RF = 10%, so the genes are 10 map units apart. Using several genes, scientists built linkage maps showing the order of genes along chromosomes — the first gene maps, made decades before DNA sequencing. RF never goes above 50%: genes very far apart behave as if they were unlinked.

Recombination matters beyond maps. By shuffling alleles, it increases genetic diversity, giving natural selection more variety to act on. Plant breeders also use it to combine useful traits, such as high yield and disease resistance in rice.

Common mistake: thinking linked genes are always inherited together. Crossing over can separate them; the closer they are, the less often it happens.

pairs.why: Recombination produces new combinations of alleles.
Linked genes sit close together on the same chromosome.
One map unit equals 1% recombination frequency.
Crossing over between homologs happens in prophase I.
RF = recombinants ÷ total × 100.
A centimorgan is another name for a map unit.
